findings.title: Backup code validation/consumption has a check-then-update race (TOCTOU)
findings.body: The backup-code login path reads `user.backupCodes`, decrypts it, checks `indexOf` for a match, then later re-encrypts and writes back the array with the used code nulled out (lines 139-156). There is no transaction, row lock, or optimistic version check between the read and the write. If two requests for the same user run concurrently (e.g. a double-submitted login or two tabs), both can read the same pre-update state, both pass the `index !== -1` check, and whichever update runs last overwrites the other's change — meaning the single-use guarantee promised by the UI text ('Each backup code can be used exactly once') can be violated: a single code can authenticate more than once, or one of two different codes used concurrently can end up still marked as unused.

findings.title: Backup codes are stored with reversible symmetric encryption instead of being hashed
findings.body: Backup codes are encrypted with `symmetricEncrypt`/`symmetricDecrypt` using `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (setup.ts line 68, next-auth-options.ts lines 140/154) rather than hashed. Unlike TOTP secrets, backup codes never need to be redisplayed after generation, so they should be hashed (similar to passwords) rather than stored reversibly. Anyone who obtains the DB plus the single symmetric encryption key (which protects many other secrets) can recover every user's plaintext backup codes, which is a stronger blast radius than necessary for a one-time-use credential.

findings.title: Backup code input has no normalization, but generated codes are lowercase hex only
findings.body: `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` (setup.ts) always produces lowercase hex characters, but the `TextField` used to collect the backup code here has no `autoCapitalize="off"`/lowercasing/trim applied, and the server-side comparison (`backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` in next-auth-options.ts and disable.ts) is an exact, case-sensitive string match. Many mobile browsers auto-capitalize the first character of a plain text input by default, and hex codes contain letters a-f roughly 37% of the time as the first character. A user who manually types a valid backup code on a mobile device can have it silently mismatched and rejected as 'incorrect', even though the code is correct.

findings.title: BackupCode component's internal function is misnamed "TwoFactor"
findings.body: This new file exports a component for displaying/collecting the backup code, but the function is declared as `export default function TwoFactor({ center = true })`, an apparent copy-paste leftover from TwoFactor.tsx. While the default export still works because callers alias the import (`import BackupCode from "@components/auth/BackupCode"`), the component will show up as "TwoFactor" in React DevTools/stack traces alongside the actual TwoFactor component, which is confusing for debugging and future maintenance.

findings.title: "missing_backup_codes" message points to a non-existent settings feature
findings.body: The new string `"missing_backup_codes": "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings."` is shown to users on login/disable when no backup codes exist, but this PR provides no settings UI or endpoint to regenerate backup codes after 2FA has been enabled — the only way to get new backup codes is to disable and re-enable 2FA entirely (which re-runs the setup flow). Telling users to 'generate them in your settings' is misleading and will create support confusion since no such control exists.

findings.title: onEnable() is no longer called immediately after 2FA is actually enabled server-side
findings.body: Previously, a successful TOTP verification called `onEnable()` immediately, letting the parent page refresh its 2FA-enabled state. Now, on success the code only does `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` (line 135); `onEnable()` is deferred until the user explicitly clicks the new 'Close' button on the backup-codes screen (around line 267). At this point 2FA is already enabled on the server (the enable API call already succeeded). If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (Escape key, clicking the overlay, closing the tab) before clicking 'Close', the parent component's `onEnable` callback never fires, leaving the UI out of sync with the backend (e.g. a toggle/switch that still shows 2FA as disabled even though it is enabled) until the page is reloaded.

findings.title: No e2e coverage added for logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
findings.body: This PR implements an entirely new authentication path (logging in via backup code) and a new disable path (disabling 2FA via backup code), but the only test addition related to these flows is a `// TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup` comment. The existing tests only exercise download/copy/close of the backup-codes dialog during setup; the actual consumption of a backup code to log in or to disable 2FA (including the single-use/invalidation behavior) is left completely untested, despite being the core new feature of this PR.

findings.title: FIXME comment added but the broken assertion is left unfixed
findings.body: A new comment at line 50-51 explicitly documents that `await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` passes even when the switch is not checked (because `.isChecked()` returns an unawaited Promise, which is always truthy). The PR acknowledges this is broken but ships it unfixed, so the 'Enable 2FA' step in this test does not actually verify that the switch became checked, reducing confidence in the enable-2FA regression coverage that this PR also modifies.

findings.title: Backup-codes download Blob URL can leak if setup is cancelled before completion
findings.body: `handleSetup` creates a Blob URL via `URL.createObjectURL` for the backup codes (lines 94-99) and only revokes the previous URL the next time `handleSetup` succeeds (`if (backupCodesUrl) URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)`). `resetState()` (line 71-75), which runs when the user clicks 'Cancel' at any step or 'Close' after viewing backup codes, does not revoke `backupCodesUrl`. If the user cancels after the password step succeeded (so a Blob URL was created) but before starting setup again, or simply finishes the flow, the object URL is never revoked and the Blob remains referenced for the lifetime of the page, which is a minor memory leak that is easy to avoid by revoking in `resetState`.
